current_abi_observations.detail: bytecodeInstruction embeds runtime.Value, strings, AST types/nodes, nested program pointers, and Go-managed metadata; bytecodeProgram embeds maps, slices, and runtime definition pointers.
runtime.Value implementations embed Go strings, slices, maps, interfaces, functions, AST pointers, environments, mutexes, contexts, condition variables, futures, and arbitrary host values.
VM frames, environments, lookup caches, iterator and loop stacks, unwind state, Array ownership, raw sidecars, and async payloads are Go object graphs.
production spawn uses goroutines, contexts, channels/conditions, and Go-owned Future state; deterministic execution resumes exact Go VM state after serial yields.
extern functions are compiled as exact-toolchain Go plugins and exchange runtime.Value/NativeCallContext state.
integer handles can keep Go values rooted across C, but each semantic operation still returns to Go and foreign memory cannot traverse the referenced Go object graph.

variants.reason: Safe handles preserve roots but cannot execute Go-owned Array, map, nominal, call, error, environment, Future, or extern semantics. Measured hot functions hit such boundaries after only four to seven primitive instructions, making this the rejected native-leaf/side-exit architecture.

Owning values, heap, environments, dispatch, errors, scheduling, and externs in C could keep whole activations native, but it creates a second semantic runtime and requires graph conversion or dual ownership at every Go/tree-walker/extern boundary.
A JIT library changes code generation but not the Go object-graph boundary; safe generated code remains a pointer-free leaf with dense exits, exactly the unadmitted native tier.

Adding a foreign heap/runtime beneath a JIT has the same semantic duplication and boundary conversion problem as a complete C runtime, plus an unselected dependency, license, code-memory, and platform policy.
Custom emitters do not alter the semantic boundary, so safe code still side-exits at the same four-to-seven-instruction spans.
A complete foreign runtime retains the duplication problem while custom per-OS/architecture emitters add the largest unwind, executable-memory, cache, security, and maintenance burden.

prototype_policy.supported_platforms: No backend-specific platform is selected. Ordinary Go bytecode remains required everywhere the native Go interpreter builds.
prototype_policy.toolchain: No new C/C++/Rust/JIT dependency is admitted.
prototype_policy.code_memory: No executable-memory or W^X policy is activated because no code-generating backend is selected.
prototype_policy.fallback: Ordinary Go bytecode remains the sole implementation and semantic authority.
prototype_policy.conformance: Existing tree-walker/bytecode fixture parity and portable application verifiers remain mandatory for any future engine.

next_lane.scope: Determine whether Able can define one backend-neutral serialized program/value/effect ABI that both the Go reference runtime and a future fast engine can implement without per-operation foreign calls or duplicate language semantics. This is a feasibility/design tranche, not a runtime rewrite.
required_outputs: an immutable serialized instruction/type/source-identity format with no Go pointers
a value, identity, mutation, root, and lifetime model covering every runtime.Value kind
semantic operation and structured effect/resume contracts for dispatch, errors, cleanup, suspension, and externs
an ownership decision for heap, GC, environments, futures, and host handles
a migration and conformance plan preserving tree-walker and ordinary-bytecode fallback
a target-budget model for at least three unlike whole hot functions
next_lane.admission: Advance only if one design keeps a single semantic authority, avoids per-opcode foreign transitions, preserves identity/fallback without whole-graph conversion, and models at least 25% target-excess reduction in three unlike applications. Otherwise close foreign/native backends and return to the portable application frontier.
next_lane.exclusions: No WASM, foreign runtime implementation, JIT dependency, executable-memory code, benchmark branches, named-container rules, or non-primitive nominal special cases.
